fields.h1: Build a Post Event Survey Tied to Who Attended What
fields.hero_description: Build a post event survey that knows who attended what, saves every answer to a database you own, and flags low scores.
fields.features_heading: What the Survey Does After the Event Ends
fields.features_subheading: Six things the survey handles, from drafting the questions to keeping the code once the event is over.
fields.feature_1:
Questions drafted from your event

Describe the event and what you plan to change next time. Emergent drafts the questions, pairing ratings with an open box, and you reword any of them with a follow-up prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Only the sessions each person attended

Pull check-in or badge scans from any event tool with an API. Each attendee then rates the sessions they walked into, and a keynote score never comes from people who skipped it.
fields.feature_3:
Every answer saved with its context

Each answer lands in a database you own, next to the person's ticket type, company, and sessions. Filter by any of them to compare first-time attendees with returning ones.
fields.feature_4:
Low scores sent to their owner

Set a threshold per owner: the program chair for sessions, sales for exhibitors, operations for the venue. Alerts arrive in Slack or email with the comment quoted in full.
fields.feature_5:
No cap on responses

Emergent puts no cap on survey responses, and a 2,000-person conference can answer without hitting a plan limit. Reminders go only to people who have not answered yet.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, your code

Host the survey on your own domain, included with Emergent and paid in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep it after the event.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Events and What Their Surveys Caught
fields.tab_content_1:
Each session scored by the people who sat in it

The morning after a conference closes, each attendee gets an email listing only the sessions their badge was scanned into. They rate each one out of 5. Any session averaging below 3.5 goes to the program chair with every comment attached. On day two, the freight forecasting panel scored 3.2 across 41 ratings.
fields.tab_content_2:
Find the exhibitors who will not rebook

Two days after the expo, every exhibitor rates booth traffic and lead quality, then answers one question: will you book again, yes, no, or not sure? Either of the last two opens a follow-up for the sales manager. Larchfield Cabinetry, in booth 214, answered not sure. Its comment: traffic died along the back wall.
fields.tab_content_3:
What registrants came for, and whether they got it

A week before a Saturday workshop, each registrant picks the topic they most want covered. The post event survey then names that pick and asks whether today covered it. Both answers sit on one registrant row. Of the 14 people who came for pricing, 5 said yes. Pricing moves to the top of the next agenda.
fields.tab_content_4:
Day one answers that change day two

After day one of a three-day festival, ticket holders get an evening email asking how long entry took. Each answer is saved with the gate from their ticket scan. Overnight, 640 answered. River Gate scored 2.1 out of 5, against 4.1 at North Gate. The operations lead added two scanners there before day two.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Post Event Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan a post event survey whose answers change what you do at the next event.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the answers will change
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about one thing at a time
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Ask for the reason behind a low score
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the decisions the survey should settle, such as whether to keep the venue or which track to cut. Every question should feed one of them. Put those decisions at the top of your prompt, and Emergent drafts questions around them.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Name the parts of the event you control: sessions, venue, catering, check-in, and the event app. Leave out what is outside your hands, like the weather or the host city. Each item on the list becomes one rating, and the list stays short.
fields.howto_step_3_des: A question that rates the food and the venue together is double-barreled. Pew Research Center notes that such questions are difficult to answer and often lead to responses that are difficult to interpret. Split them, and put the overall rating first, since question order can influence how people respond.
fields.howto_step_4_des: When someone rates a session 2 or lower, show a follow-up box that asks what went wrong. The reason sits next to the score in the table. A speaker can fix a slow demo, but nobody can act on a bare 2.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Test it with a fake attendee
fields.howto_step_5_des: Register a test attendee, scan them into two sessions, and send yourself the survey. Check that only those two sessions appear and that each answer lands in the table. Then rate one session low and confirm the alert reaches its owner.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Word the overall rating and the would-you-return question the same way every year. Small wording differences can change the answers people give, and a reworded question breaks the comparison with last year. Reword the other questions as freely as you like.
fields.howto_step_7_des: When registration for the next event opens, tell past respondents what their answers changed, such as a longer lunch break or a session moved to a bigger room. Tie each fix to the question that raised it, and keep the note short enough to read on a phone.

faq_plan.q: What are good post-event survey questions?
faq_plan.ref: What are good post-event survey questions?

prov.original: What are good post-event survey questions?

faq_plan.a: Good post event survey questions are short, specific, and about something the person experienced, like a session they sat in or the line at check-in. Use one rating scale throughout so scores compare across sessions. Leave out anything the person could not judge, such as the event budget or the choice of caterer.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a post event survey?
faq_plan.a: Describe the event, who attended, and what you want to learn in a prompt. Emergent's AI survey builder drafts the questions, the send time, and the table that stores every answer. Publish it, then share the link by email or on a QR code printed on signs at the exits.

faq_plan.q: What should an event feedback form include?
faq_plan.a: An event feedback form needs a few fields besides the questions: the person's role (attendee, speaker, or exhibitor), the sessions they attended, and a checkbox asking whether you may follow up. Those fields let you split answers by group and reply to complaints. Keep the form short enough to finish on a phone.

faq_plan.q: Should an event feedback survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Make it anonymous when the questions judge people, and named when you need to follow up. A named event feedback survey lets you call back an unhappy exhibitor or tie each answer to the sessions someone attended. A church survey that asks about a pastor is a good case for anonymity; feedback on a parish picnic can carry names.

faq_plan.q: What are good pre event survey questions?
faq_plan.a: Good pre event survey questions ask what people want from the event while you can still plan for it. Ask which topic they most want covered, any dietary or access needs, and which sessions they plan to attend. Their answers set room sizes and catering counts, and give the post event survey something to check against.

faq_plan.q: When should you send after event survey questions?
faq_plan.a: Send after event survey questions within a day of the close, while people still remember which sessions they sat through. For a multi-day event, a short survey each evening catches problems you can still fix the next morning. Send one reminder to anyone who has not answered after three days.

faq_plan.q: What are some examples of post event survey questions?
faq_plan.a: Five that fit a conference or a trade show: How would you rate the event overall? Which session will you use at work? Was anything hard to find, such as rooms or food? Would you come next year? What one change would you make? For a paid event, add the value question a customer feedback survey would ask: was the ticket worth the price?

faq_plan.q: Should post event survey questions for attendees differ from those for speakers?
faq_plan.ref: post event survey questions for attendees
faq_plan.a: Yes. Attendees judge content, logistics, and value for the ticket, while speakers judge the room, the audio setup, and the audience they got. Send each group its own short version, and tag every answer with the group so you can read them apart. Emergent builds every version in one app, with no cap on how many responses come in.

faq_plan.q: Is there an event feedback survey template you can start from?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Describe your event in a prompt, such as a two-day conference with 30 sessions and 40 exhibitors, and Emergent drafts a starting template: questions, rating scales, and the table behind them. Rename a session, add a question, or split the survey by audience with a follow-up prompt instead of editing each field.

faq_plan.q: What is an event satisfaction survey?
faq_plan.a: An event satisfaction survey measures how satisfied people were with one event, through an overall score and a rating for each part. It is shorter than a full post event survey, and repeating it after every event lets you compare scores over time. For a company offsite, keep it apart from an employee satisfaction survey, which asks about the job, not the day.

plan.angle: The top 10 is question lists (SurveyMonkey, Qualtrics, Bizzabo, Swapcard, Formbricks, MPI) plus one Microsoft Forms template. None ties an answer to what the person actually attended, and none shows who acts on a low score. This page answers the question-list intent in the FAQ (good questions, examples, pre-event and attendee questions, timing, templates) and then shows four post event surveys built from a prompt: session ratings matched to badge scans, an exhibitor rebooking survey, a pre and post pair on one registrant row, and a nightly festival survey that fixes day two. The post-webinar sibling owns webinars; this page owns in-person events.
